questions.question: What is java.nio.file.Path and how do you create one?
questions.title: Path and Paths.get()
questions.direct_answer: Path is an interface representing a file system path; create instances using Path.of() (Java 11+) or Paths.get() (Java 7+), which accept a string path or URI.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the modern NIO2 path creation API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using new File('path') instead of Path.of('path') in modern Java code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Path is an interface—different implementations exist for different file systems (local, zip, in-memory)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: java.nio.file.Path is an interface introduced in Java 7 as part of the NIO2 API. Unlike java.io.File which is a class, Path is an interface, which means there can be different implementations—the default implementation for the local file system, but also implementations for zip file systems, in-memory file systems, or remote file systems through custom providers. To create a Path, you have two main options. In Java 7+: Paths.get('/home/user/data.txt') or Paths.get('/home/user', 'data.txt')—you can pass multiple segments and they're joined with the OS separator. In Java 11+: Path.of('/home/user/data.txt')—a static factory method added directly to the interface, more idiomatic. Both produce equivalent objects. You can also resolve relative paths: basePath.resolve('subdir/file.txt') appends the relative path to the base. Path.toFile() converts back to java.io.File if needed for legacy APIs. Unlike File, Path doesn't make any OS calls just from being created—it's just a representation of a path string.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Path is an interface (not a class like File)—enables different file system implementations
Paths.get('path', 'subpath') (Java 7+) or Path.of('path') (Java 11+)
path.resolve('relative/path') appends relative path to base path
path.toFile() converts to legacy java.io.File when needed
Creating a Path makes no OS calls—no existence check
Path.getFileName(), getParent(), getRoot() for path components

questions.question: What are the most important methods in the java.nio.file.Files utility class?
questions.title: Files Utility Class Key Methods
questions.direct_answer: Key Files methods include: readAllBytes/readAllLines/readString for reading, writeString/write for writing, copy/move for file operations, createDirectory/createDirectories for directories, exists/isFile/isDirectory for checks, and delete for removal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with the modern Java file operation API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Files exists and implementing verbose manual IO for simple operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Files.copy() with StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING and StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES options

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Files is a utility class with static methods for all common file operations—think of it as the Swiss Army knife of Java file IO. For reading: Files.readAllBytes(path) for binary, Files.readAllLines(path) for all text lines as List<String>, Files.readString(path) for all text as a single String (Java 11+). For writing: Files.writeString(path, string) or Files.write(path, bytes/lines). For file operations: Files.copy(source, target) to copy files, Files.move(source, target) to move/rename—both accept copy options like StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING. For directory creation: Files.createDirectory(path) for one level, Files.createDirectories(path) for full path. For checking: Files.exists(path), Files.isFile(path), Files.isDirectory(path), Files.size(path). For deletion: Files.delete(path) throws exception if it fails, or Files.deleteIfExists(path). For streaming: Files.lines(path) for lazy line-by-line reading, Files.list(path) for directory listing, Files.walk(path) for recursive traversal. Every method throws IOException on failure—proper error handling unlike the old boolean-return File methods.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Read: readAllBytes(), readAllLines(), readString() (Java 11+), lines() (lazy stream)
Write: writeString(), write(path, bytes), write(path, lines)
File ops: copy(), move() with StandardCopyOption options
Directories: createDirectory(), createDirectories()
Checks: exists(), isFile(), isDirectory(), size()
Delete: delete() throws on failure, deleteIfExists() returns boolean
All methods throw IOException—proper error handling

questions.question: How do you traverse a directory recursively using Files.walk() in Java?
questions.title: Directory Traversal with Files.walk()
questions.direct_answer: Files.walk(path) returns a depth-first Stream<Path> of all files and directories starting from the given path; filter with stream operations and use try-with-resources to close the stream and release the directory handle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical NIO2 knowledge for directory operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not closing the stream returned by Files.walk()—it holds an open directory handle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Files.walk(path, maxDepth) to limit traversal depth and Files.find() for combined walk+filter

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Files.walk(path) returns a lazy Stream<Path> that performs depth-first traversal of the directory tree starting at the given path, including the path itself. The stream yields directories and files mixed in depth-first order. A common pattern is to filter for only files and process them: try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(baseDir)) { paths.filter(Files::isRegularFile).filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith('.txt')).forEach(this::processFile); }. The try-with-resources is critical—Files.walk() holds open directory handles for each level of traversal and they must be released. To limit depth: Files.walk(path, 2) only goes 2 levels deep. Files.find(path, maxDepth, BiPredicate) is an alternative that combines the walk with a filter predicate, and can be more efficient because it doesn't yield paths that don't match. For just direct children without recursion, use Files.list(path). To find all files of a certain extension recursively, Files.walk combined with stream filtering is the idiomatic NIO2 approach.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Files.walk(path): lazy Stream<Path>, depth-first, includes starting path itself
MUST use try-with-resources—stream holds open directory handles
Filter: .filter(Files::isRegularFile) to exclude directories
Limit depth: Files.walk(path, maxDepth)
Files.list(path): direct children only (no recursion), also needs try-with-resources
Files.find(path, depth, BiPredicate): combined walk+filter, potentially more efficient

questions.question: How do Path.resolve(), relativize(), and normalize() work?
questions.title: Path.resolve(), relativize(), normalize()
questions.direct_answer: resolve() appends a path to another; relativize() computes the relative path from one path to another; normalize() removes redundant . and .. elements from a path.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to build paths with string concatenation instead of using resolve()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete use case for relativize()—generating relative links in file-based content systems

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These three methods cover the most common path manipulation operations. resolve() appends a path: Path.of('/home/user').resolve('documents/file.txt') gives /home/user/documents/file.txt. If you resolve an absolute path onto another path, the result is just the absolute path—resolve('/etc/config') gives /etc/config regardless of base. relativize() is the inverse: it computes the relative path from one path to another. Path.of('/a/b').relativize(Path.of('/a/b/c/d')) gives c/d—the relative path to walk from /a/b to /a/b/c/d. Useful for generating relative links or relative import paths. normalize() removes redundant elements: Path.of('/home/user/../user/documents').normalize() gives /home/user/documents. It doesn't make system calls—it just operates on the string representation. For the real resolved path including symlinks, use toRealPath() which does make system calls. A common security pattern: resolve() a user-provided path onto a base directory, then check that normalize().startsWith(baseDir) to prevent directory traversal attacks.

sections.title: Key Points
content: resolve(other): append relative path to base path
resolve(absolute): returns the absolute path (not appended)
relativize(target): compute relative path from this path to target
normalize(): remove . and .. components from path string
normalize() is string-only—no OS calls; toRealPath() resolves symlinks with OS call
Security: resolve + normalize + startsWith check prevents directory traversal

questions.question: What is WatchService in Java NIO2 and what is it used for?
questions.title: WatchService for File System Monitoring
questions.direct_answer: WatchService is a NIO2 API that monitors a directory for changes (file created, modified, deleted) and delivers events; used in applications that react to file system changes like hot-reload configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of a NIO2 feature with no java.io.File equivalent
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing WatchService exists and suggesting polling with Files.exists() in a loop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring Boot's DevTools uses WatchService internally for hot-reload, and configuration libraries like Typesafe Config

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: WatchService is a NIO2 API introduced in Java 7 that lets you register a directory to receive notifications when files inside it are created, modified, or deleted. The API works by registering a Path with the WatchService for specific events: dir.register(watchService, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE, ENTRY_MODIFY, ENTRY_DELETE). You then poll the WatchService in a loop: WatchKey key = watchService.take() blocks until an event occurs, then you iterate over key.pollEvents() to get the individual events. Each event has a kind (created/modified/deleted) and a context (the filename). After processing, you reset the key so it can receive more events. Real-world uses: Spring Boot DevTools watches your classpath for changes and hot-reloads classes when source is compiled. Configuration libraries watch for config file changes and reload without restart. File upload processors watch an inbox directory for new files. IDE plugins watch source files for external changes. The WatchService uses OS-native file watching APIs (inotify on Linux, FSEvents on macOS) so it's efficient—not polling.

sections.title: Key Points
content: WatchService: register directory → receive events for ENTRY_CREATE, ENTRY_MODIFY, ENTRY_DELETE
dir.register(watchService, StandardWatchEventKinds.*) to subscribe
watchService.take(): blocks until event occurs
key.pollEvents(): get individual file change events
Must call key.reset() to receive future events on same key
Uses OS-native notifications (inotify, FSEvents)—not polling
Used by: Spring DevTools, config reload libraries, file inbox processors
